s01_intro: Laser cutting starts with a flat, two-dimensional drawing. In this tutorial, you'll build exactly that: a basic sketch in Onshape that's ready for the laser cutter at Nolop. We'll draw a simple bracket plate, drive its size from exact numbers, add a bolt hole, and export a D X F file.
s02_documents: Onshape runs in your browser, so there is nothing to install. Sign in with your Tufts account to get the free education plan. This is your documents page. Every design you make is stored here. Click Create, then Document, and give it a name.
s03_partstudio: Onshape opens a Part Studio. Think of it as a workbench. The list on the left is the feature list. Every step you take is recorded there, in order, so you can go back and change any number later. In the middle is your 3D workspace. Every part starts life as a sketch: a two-dimensional drawing on a flat plane.
s04_sketch: Click the Sketch tool in the toolbar, then choose which plane to draw on. For laser-cut parts, the Top plane is a good habit. It's flat, and it maps cleanly onto a sheet of material. Pick Top, and the sketch opens ready to draw.
s05_normal: Right now we're looking at the sketch plane from an angle. Press the N key to look straight at it. This is how your part will sit on the laser bed: flat, and square to the screen.
s06_rectangle: Pick the Rectangle tool, or just press G. Click once to set the first corner, then click again for the opposite corner. Onshape adds dimensions as you draw. Don't worry about where you click, or how big it is. The next step is the one that matters.
s07_dimensions: This is the most important habit in the whole tutorial. Never accept a random size. Click the horizontal dimension and type the real number: one hundred millimetres. Then tab to the vertical dimension and type sixty. Press Enter. Onshape rebuilds the shape to match exactly what you typed. The drawing is now driven by your measurements, not by mouse movement.
s08_circle: Most laser-cut parts need a hole. Pick the Circle tool, or press C, and click the approximate location of where the hole goes. We'll position it accurately next. Here's how. Dimension the circle to the diameter of your bolt, and dimension its position from the edges. Same habit: type real numbers. If you measured six millimetres, type six.
s09_finish: When every dimension is set, the sketch turns black. That means it is fully constrained: locked down, and predictable. Click the green check to close the sketch. Your drawing is stored in the feature list, and you can reopen it at any time.
s10_dxf: For the laser cutter, you need a D X F file. Right-click the sketch in the feature list, and choose Export as D X F. Save it, and take it to Nolop, where it gets imported in Inkscape. There, red lines cut and black lines sketch. That side of the process is covered in a separate video. That's the whole loop: measure the real part, draw it in Onshape, export the file, and cut.
s11_recap: Quick recap. Start a sketch on the Top plane. Draw with the rectangle and circle tools. Always drive the shape with real numbers, not the mouse. Then export a D X F and cut it. Happy making.
